name: American Parliamentary Debate (APDA and NPDA)
summary: Two teams of two, Government and Opposition, debate a motion with short preparation and no published evidence in the round, relying on reasoning, general knowledge and wit.
who: College students through the American Parliamentary Debate Association (APDA, mostly at colleges in the eastern United States) and the National Parliamentary Debate Association (NPDA, nationwide). Many high school leagues offer a parliamentary event too.
resolution: A new motion each round. In NPDA it is announced twenty minutes before the round. In APDA the government often writes its own case; at "motions" tournaments both teams get a motion and fifteen minutes.

speeches.name: Prime Minister Constructive
speeches.job: Interpret the motion and present the government case.

speeches.name: Leader of the Opposition Constructive
speeches.job: Answer the case and present the opposition's arguments.

speeches.name: Member of Government Constructive
speeches.job: Rebuild the government case, answer the opposition, and add arguments.

speeches.name: Member of the Opposition Constructive
speeches.job: The opposition's last constructive; it sets up the opposition rebuttal.

speeches.name: Leader of the Opposition Rebuttal
speeches.job: Sum up why the opposition wins. No new arguments.

speeches.name: Prime Minister Rebuttal
speeches.job: Sum up why the government wins. It may answer new arguments made in the MOC, and nothing else new.

prep.note: No prep time between speeches. NPDA: twenty minutes from the motion's announcement to the round, with any printed or electronic materials; after that, only handwritten notes. APDA: fifteen minutes (the opposition's prep after hearing the case, or both teams at motions tournaments).

poi.note: Points of information are allowed in constructive speeches except in the first and last minute, and are short questions of under 15 seconds. In rebuttals, a debater may raise a point of order to object to a new argument.

grace.note: APDA's rulebook allows up to 30 seconds beyond each speech's time (for example, 7:30 for the PMC).

rewards: Logic and analysis over quoted evidence
Broad general knowledge of history, economics and current events
Quick thinking, humor and clear speaking
Good use of points of information
start: Read widely: a good newspaper and an introductory economics book help as much as anything.
Practice twenty-minute prep with a partner and a legal pad.
Practice the rebuttals: four or five minutes, only what's already in the round, weighed.
Ask your college team about novice tournaments.
varies: Prep: twenty minutes in NPDA; fifteen minutes in APDA.
Who chooses the topic: NPDA announces a motion each round; APDA often lets the government write its own case.
Grace time: APDA allows 30 seconds beyond each speech's time; NPDA does not list grace time.
High school parliamentary leagues set their own times and rules.

p: The government proposes a case for the motion; the opposition argues against it. There is no cross-examination period. Instead, during the middle minutes of constructive speeches, the other team can rise for a short point of information.
Debaters may not read published evidence in the round, so arguments stand or fall on their reasoning and on facts any well-read person knows.

sources.title: American Parliamentary Debate Association Rulebook (as of the 2025-2026 season)

topicShort: A new motion each round (APDA: often the government’s own case)
